raw_response:
Looking at my land and my situation, I don't need to think too hard about this. My family has farmed here in Quzhou for three generations. The soil here, the weather, the markets — I know them. The answer is what it has always been: winter wheat, then summer maize on the same ground. That rotation works. It feeds us, it pays the bills, and I can manage it myself without relying too much on hired help, which gets expensive and harder to find every year.

I have 8 mu. All of it goes into wheat this October and maize the following June right after harvest. I won't try cotton or vegetables — that's for younger people or those with connections to buy-back contracts. I'm 64. I want predictable work and predictable income.

For wheat, I'll use the improved variety the village extension station recommended last year — Kenong 199 or something similar. Not the old seeds from my own stock; yields are noticeably lower and I know it. I'll rotary-till before sowing to break up the hard layer from summer. I'll apply compound fertilizer at sowing and topdress urea at jointing. Four irrigations: before sowing to ensure germination, before winter freeze, at jointing, and at heading. I won't skip the heading irrigation — that's where I lose yield if I cut corners. Two pesticide passes: one for aphids in spring, one fungicide near heading.

For maize, I'll direct-seed right after the wheat combine passes through — no-tillage, it saves me two days of hard labor in the June heat and my back isn't what it was. I'll use Zhengdan 958 hybrid seed, same as last year. Two irrigations — one at knee-high if it's dry, one at tasseling. One pesticide pass for corn borer. I apply the fertilizer in two shots: a bit at sowing, the rest at big bell stage.
